title: Grok Bot reception: teammate pitch, independent caveats, chatbot confusion
summary: Two days after launch, coverage agrees on the job: Grok Bot is a persistent worker with its own cloud computer, not a chat window that stops when you close the laptop. Product press leans on the teammate metaphor. Independent writeups accept the pitch and then ask about shared-machine risk, bundle pricing, and the name collision with Grok the chatbot. This brief is a reading of public coverage, not a usage report.

sections.heading: What product press is saying
bullets: xAI’s own introduction frames Grok Bot as always-on agents that keep a dedicated cloud computer, sign into the tools you already use, and return when the work is done or a decision is needed.
The Verge treats the launch as a teammate product rather than a new chatbot: you assign work, the bot stays on the job after you step away, and multiple bots can coordinate in a shared thread.

Access is described as a beta bundled into existing high-tier plans (SuperGrok Heavy, Cursor Ultra, Cursor Teams Premium), not as a standalone SKU. Enterprise is a waitlist in the launch copy, not a general-availability claim.

The official story emphasizes internal prototype use (sales outreach, marketing, office ops, bug fixes) and the ability to follow along once, save a routine, and rerun it. Those are product claims, not third-party measured outcomes.

sources.label: The Verge: Grok is now an AI teammate you can assign work

sections.heading: Independent takes
bullets: Hands-on and explainer pieces (Digital Trends and longer product reviews in the same vein as Continuum-style writeups) repeat the same distinction: the chatbot answers; the bot is supposed to finish the job on a machine that keeps running.
The useful independent questions are operational, not theatrical: one shared cloud computer per account, so files, browser sessions, and logins can be visible across every bot on that account.

Reviewers also flag the bundle: this is not priced as a cheap add-on. If you are already on a qualifying Cursor or SuperGrok plan, the experiment is incremental. If you are not, the seat cost is the first filter.

None of the pieces cited here publish audited task-completion rates, error rates, or hours-saved figures. Treat any numeric productivity claim you see elsewhere as unverified unless a source shows its method.

sources.label: Digital Trends: Grok Bot wants to take work off your plate

sections.heading: Brand confusion with the Grok chatbot
bullets: The name does most of the damage. People who already use Grok as a chat model will hear “Grok Bot” as a skin, a mobile wrapper, or a new personality, not as a separate product with a computer, connectors, and approval gates.

A practical test for SMB ops: if the task dies when the chat tab closes, you wanted the chatbot. If the task should keep going overnight inside email, CRM, or a browser session, you are talking about the bot.
Internal language should stay literal. Say “assign the inbox bot” or “ask Grok in chat,” not “have Grok handle it,” until the team can hear the difference without a lecture.
Security conversations should start from the shared-machine model in public coverage, not from chatbot data-retention folklore. The blast radius is the accounts you sign the computer into.

bottomLine: Read Grok Bot as a delegated worker on a shared cloud machine, bundled into expensive existing seats, not as “Grok with extra steps.” Pilot one bounded workflow (a morning digest, a CRM cleanup, a watch-the-inbox job) with approvals left on. Keep chatbot Q&A and bot tasking as two different sentences. Do not staff a process on launch anecdotes or unsourced productivity numbers.
